name: Saltgrave Denim Chore Coat
description:
A four-pocket chore coat in 14oz raw indigo denim, cut boxy and slightly long in a French workwear tradition. The construction is triple-stitched throughout in gold thread, with bartacks at every stress point and a lining of natural cotton twill that breathes better than most tech fabrics. Saltgrave is a small independent label — two people, a press, and a roster of specialty fabric suppliers — making a handful of pieces per run that sell out in days through their direct channel.

This jacket has no branding visible from the outside. If you know Saltgrave, you recognize the distinctive pocket placement and the custom shank buttons. If you don't, it just looks like a very well-made denim jacket worn by someone who has good taste and doesn't announce it. It fades spectacularly with wear — the creases go white, the body deepens, and after a year it looks like something that cost three times as much.
what_it_says: You know things about clothing that most people don't. You found this without being told to find it. That matters to you.
story_hooks: The two founders of Saltgrave have gone silent — their direct channel is dark, the last run was never shipped, and the people who pre-ordered are getting increasingly worried about more than their money.
A Saltgrave chore coat appears in an archival photo from 2187 — thirteen years before the brand was founded — worn by someone who looks identical to one of its current owners.

A limited run of Saltgrave coats was dyed using indigo from a specific urban farm in the Shelf district; that farm has since been razed, and someone is willing to pay extraordinary amounts for any piece from that batch.
